cards.title: Recognizable separability of automatic relations
cards.formal: Is the following recognizable-separability problem undecidable, as asserted by Conjecture 7.1 of the source? Given a finite alphabet \(A\) and two nondeterministic finite automata representing binary automatic relations \(R_1,R_2\subseteq A^*\times A^*\), decide whether there exist \(k\in\mathbb N\) and regular languages \(L_1,\ldots,L_k,K_1,\ldots,K_k\subseteq A^*\) with \[R_1\subseteq S,\qquad S\cap R_2=\varnothing,\qquad S=\bigcup_{i=1}^{k}(L_i\times K_i).\] The number \(k\) and the sizes of all component automata have no prescribed finite bound. Undecidability means that no deterministic Turing machine halts and gives the correct answer on every finite input description of this kind.

source_formulation.text: The Rec-separability problem – or, equivalently, the regular colorability problem – is undecidable.
source_formulation.caption: Conjecture 7.1, source statement; MFCS 2023, p. 17:13

cards.why: Automatic relations allow a finite machine to compare positions in two unbounded strings. Recognizable relations replace this synchronization with finitely many independent regular tests. Deciding whether such a replacement can separate two specifications is a basic abstraction question connected to regular colorings of infinite graphs and to simplifying relational constraints. Its answer would locate an effective boundary between two elementary finite descriptions of infinite relations.
cards.status_note: Source-open: the MFCS 2023 statement is Conjecture 7.1, not a theorem. Morvan’s 22 May 2025 thesis retains the unrestricted question as Open Problem VII.1.10. The February 2026 automatic-structure dichotomy concerns a fixed finite target and does not resolve the existentially unbounded separator size. Checked on 15 September 2026 with a bounded later-work search; no cited proof was independently formalized.

progress.text: Theorem 3.1 gives polynomial-time reductions in both directions between binary recognizable separation and finite regular colorability of automatic graphs. Theorems 4.4 and 5.6 prove undecidability for each fixed color or product bound of at least two; Conjecture 7.1 proposes undecidability for unrestricted separation.
Morvan’s thesis, Open Problem VII.1.10 and Chapter X.1, explicitly says the unrestricted recognizable-separability problem remains open.

Cuvelier and Morvan’s preprint gives a decidability dichotomy for homomorphisms from automatic structures to a fixed finite target, including the regular-homomorphism variant. Fixing that target fixes the palette in coloring instances; the result does not decide whether some finite palette exists.

The conjecture, complete binary-relation definitions, and later thesis and preprint scopes were checked. A bounded search found no resolution of the unrestricted target; the source conjecture is not presented as an established undecidability theorem.

sentences: Binary automatic relations are recognized by finite automata reading padded pairs of words synchronously.
The question asks whether it is undecidable to separate two such relations by a finite union of products of regular languages.
The number of products is existentially chosen with no prescribed upper bound.
Fixed-bound separation is already undecidable, but the unrestricted problem remains explicitly open in the checked later thesis.
A resolution would clarify when synchronized infinite relations admit effective separation by finitely many independent regular tests.

cards.definitions: For \(u,v\in A^*\), their convolution \(u\otimes v\) has length \(\max\{|u|,|v|\}\). Its \(j\)-th symbol is the pair of \(j\)-th letters, using a fresh padding symbol \(\bot\notin A\) when \(j\) exceeds one word's length. Padding occurs only at the end of the shorter component; \(\varepsilon\otimes\varepsilon=\varepsilon\). An input automaton \(B\) over \((A\cup\{\bot\})^2\) represents \(R(B)=\{(u,v):B\text{ accepts }u\otimes v\}\). Only valid convolutions affect this relation. A nondeterministic finite automaton has a finite state set, designated initial and accepting state sets, and a finite letter-labeled transition relation; it accepts a finite word if some path with that label leads from an initial state to an accepting state. A language is regular if some such automaton accepts it. A recognizable binary relation is a finite union of Cartesian products of two regular languages, as displayed above; \(k=0\) gives the empty relation. All alphabets, state sets and transition lists are explicit finite input data, with symbol and state indices encoded as binary integers with delimiters. Both relations are binary, as in the source's main formulation; neither has to be symmetric. There is no promise that they are disjoint. The quantifier over candidate separators is inside the decision problem and ranges over all finite descriptions; it is not a fixed bound supplied to the deciding machine. One uniform machine would have to decide every instance, using finite computation and no advice or oracle. No complexity bound is requested.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that the defined input language is undecidable, or refute the conjecture by supplying a uniform total decision algorithm and proving its correctness and termination in Lean. A proof of undecidability must exclude every total computable decider for unrestricted finite recognizable separators. Undecidability when the number of Cartesian products is fixed, or when the input relations are asynchronous rational relations, does not prove this conjecture.

context_blocks.text: A synchronous automaton can inspect matching positions in the two component words. In one Cartesian product, by contrast, the first component is checked independently of the second. Taking finitely many such products allows finitely many alternatives, while retaining independent tests within each alternative.

Separation permits an overapproximation: the separator may contain pairs outside both input relations. This differs from asking whether one automatic relation is itself recognizable, which is already decidable. The difference is the freedom to choose what happens on pairs not constrained by either input.

The source connects unrestricted recognizable separation to coloring an automatic graph with finitely many colors, each color class a regular language. An automatic graph has words as vertices and a synchronously recognized edge relation; adjacent vertices must receive different colors. The number of colors is existentially chosen and unbounded.

The published fixed-product-count and fixed-color-count undecidability results do not settle the unrestricted question. A pair with no separator of one prescribed size may have a larger separator. Morvan’s later thesis continues to identify this unbounded version as an open problem.

cards.title: Polynomial-time universality for unambiguous context-free grammars
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that decides whether \(L(G)=\Sigma^{*}\) for every context-free grammar \(G\) promised to be unambiguous, in time polynomial in the bit length of its explicit description? The algorithm must have one polynomial running-time bound on all input strings; correctness is required on the promised grammars. The terminal alphabet is part of the input. This card selects the polynomial-time endpoint of the source’s broader question about the exact complexity.
cards.why: Unique parse trees suffice to make universality decidable, but they do not give deterministic control of parsing. A polynomial-time procedure, or a proof excluding one, would locate the computational cost of this fundamental coverage test between finite-state reasoning and general context-free behavior.
cards.status_note: The 2019 question asks to close the complexity gap. Primary papers from 2020 and 2023 give successively stronger upper bounds, the latter in coRP with a PP oracle. A bounded search on 13 September 2026 found no resolution of the deterministic polynomial-time endpoint; this is not exhaustive current-openness certification.

definitions: A context-free grammar is a finite tuple \(G=(V,\Sigma,P,S)\), where the finite sets of nonterminals \(V\) and terminals \(\Sigma\) are disjoint, \(S\in V\), and \(P\subseteq V\times(V\cup\Sigma)^{*}\) is a finite set of production rules. The alphabet is finite and nonempty. All symbols, productions and right-hand-side strings are listed explicitly with delimited binary indices; repeated identical rules are treated as a single rule. Empty right-hand sides and unit productions are allowed.

A parse tree is a finite ordered rooted tree with root \(S\). Each nonterminal node expands according to one production, with its children in the right-hand-side order; an empty production contributes no terminal. Its yield is the terminal string read from left to right. \(L(G)\) is the set of yields. The unambiguity promise says that each word has at most one such parse tree, including the empty word. It is a promise on the given grammar, not merely on its language.

Universality includes every finite word, including \(\varepsilon\). Polynomial time means that there exist one deterministic multitape Turing machine and constants \(C,d\geq1\) whose runtime on every string of length \(N\) is at most \(C(N+1)^{d}\). It outputs a bit. On every well-formed unambiguous grammar this bit is 1 exactly for universal grammars; on other inputs either answer is allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: A complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of the specified uniform polynomial-time promise algorithm, or a Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm exists. A faster superpolynomial algorithm, a conditional lower bound alone, or an algorithm limited to deterministic grammars does not meet this criterion.

context_blocks.text: The 2019 problem asks to close the complexity gap for universality with a unique-parse promise. The benchmark’s yes/no polynomial-time endpoint is an editorial choice; a negative answer would leave finer complexity classification open.

Clemente’s 2020 paper proves a polynomial-space upper bound (Theorem 10). Its quantitative coin-flip-measure hardness theorem concerns a different problem and does not establish an equivalent hardness result for universality.

The 2023 paper improves the checked upper bound to \(\mathrm{coRP}^{\mathrm{PP}}\): randomized polynomial time with one-sided error and access to an oracle for majority acceptance of polynomial-time nondeterministic computations. This oracle-assisted bound does not provide the deterministic polynomial-time algorithm asked for here.

cards.title: Decidability of discounted-sum universality over infinite words
cards.formal: Is there an algorithm that, given a complete nondeterministic discounted-sum automaton \(\mathcal A\) with rational weights and a rational discount factor \(0<\lambda<1\), and a rational threshold \(t\), decides whether \(\mathcal A(w)\leq t\) for every infinite word \(w\in\Sigma^\omega\)? Here \(\mathcal A(w)\) is the infimum of the discounted sums of its runs on \(w\).
cards.why: Universality asks whether a quantitative finite-state specification can keep every possible infinite input below a threshold. Its decidability is a basic unresolved boundary for verification with rational discounting, where arbitrarily small tail contributions can still decide exact threshold equality.
cards.status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. Each infinite word receives the minimum cost among its runs, using one rational discount multiplier.

cards.definitions: The input contains a finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\), finite nonempty state set \(Q\), initial state \(q_0\), finite transition set \(E\subseteq Q\times\Sigma\times Q\), and weight map \(g:E\to\mathbb Q\). Completeness means every state has at least one outgoing transition for each letter. There are no epsilon transitions, final-state restrictions or fairness conditions: every infinite run is eligible. On \(w=a_0a_1\cdots\), a run is an infinite state sequence \(q_0,q_1,\ldots\) with \(e_i=(q_i,a_i,q_{i+1})\in E\). Its value is \(\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\lambda^i g(e_i)\); finite weights and \(0<\lambda<1\) ensure absolute convergence. The word value is \(\mathcal A(w)=\inf\{\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\lambda^i g(e_i): (e_i)_{i\geq0}\text{ is a run on }w\}\). The run set is nonempty and finitely branching, and this infimum is attained, so universality is equivalently \(\forall w\,\exists r\) with run value at most \(t\). Different words may use different runs; a run is not required to be chosen by an online strategy. One common discount factor applies to every transition. It is an input rational, not restricted to the reciprocal of an integer. All finite sets and tables are explicit; rational numerators and positive denominators are binary integers. An algorithm means one ordinary deterministic Turing machine that halts on every encoded valid instance and answers the exact non-strict threshold question. No finite-word truncation, approximation tolerance or bound on running time is imposed.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a terminating decision algorithm for the stated infinite-word, non-strict universality problem, including its correctness on every rational input. Alternatively prove in Lean that no such algorithm exists. A procedure for deterministic or functional automata, integer-reciprocal discount factors, finite words, strict inequalities alone or thresholds separated by a promised positive gap does not meet this full target without a proved reduction.

context_blocks.text: Discounting reduces the influence of distant transitions while retaining their exact contribution. For instance, an infinite run of weight one at every step has value \(1/(1-\lambda)\). A finite prefix determines an approximation, but equality to a rational threshold can depend on the entire continuation.

The 2014 source mentions universality as an unresolved problem related to exact-value discounted-sum games. This card fixes the standard non-strict infimum convention from the cited discounted-automata literature. The games problem is related but has different quantifiers and is not substituted for automaton universality.

Boker and Henzinger define universality by comparing every word value to a constant threshold. Their discount parameter is greater than one and divides the weight at each successive position; the present multiplier is its reciprocal. Their integral-parameter determinization result therefore covers integer-reciprocal multipliers, not all rational multipliers.

Nondeterminism is resolved separately for each complete word. Requiring one strategy to choose transitions from prefixes would impose an additional online restriction. Similarly, finding one favorable path in the underlying weighted graph would ignore the requirement to handle every input word.

The 2025 target-sum paper distinguishes strict from non-strict universality and finite from infinite words. Its universality and inclusion decidability theorem for functional automata appears in the finite-word part. Functional means that all accepting runs of each word have the same value; this is an additional restriction absent here.

For infinite words, the same paper develops connections to exact target discounted sums, including a hardness implication for strict universality and a result for instances where the corresponding generalized target sum has no solution. These are useful delineations of the remaining difficulty, rather than a decision theorem for every instance in this card.

cards.title: Zeroness of rational weighted context-free grammars
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that always halts and decides whether \(f_G(w)=0\) for every finite word \(w\in\Sigma^{*}\), given a context-free grammar in the weighted normal form below with rational production weights? sentences: A weighted context-free grammar assigns each word the sum of the weights of its parse trees.
This card asks whether an algorithm can always decide if that value is zero for every finite word.
Production weights are signed rationals, and an explicit normal form ensures every word has only finitely many parses.
The challenge is cancellation for each ordered word; results on commuting-variable series and weighted parallel processes address different models.

definitions: The input has finite disjoint sets of nonterminals \(V\) and terminals \(\Sigma\), with \(\Sigma\ne\varnothing\), a start nonterminal \(S\in V\), and finitely many productions. Every production has one of the forms \(A\to BC\) or \(A\to a\), with \(A,B,C\in V\) and \(a\in\Sigma\); additionally \(S\to\varepsilon\) is allowed. The start symbol never occurs on a right-hand side. Each production has a rational weight, explicitly encoded by a signed binary numerator and a positive binary denominator. At most one production with each left- and right-hand side is listed. There are no unit productions or other empty productions. Zero weights are allowed.

A parse tree is a finite ordered tree rooted at \(S\). Each nonterminal node expands by a listed production; the terminal leaves in order give its yield, and the empty start production gives the empty yield. The weight of a tree is the product of all weights of the productions used at its nonterminal nodes. The same production used at several nodes contributes one factor for every occurrence.

For a nonempty word of length \(m\), a parse tree in this form has \(m\) terminal-producing nodes and \(m-1\) binary-producing nodes. Thus there are only finitely many parses for each word, even when the grammar is ambiguous. Their rational weights are summed to define \(f_G(w)\); an empty sum is zero. For the empty word the value is the weight of \(S\to\varepsilon\), or zero if that production is absent. No analytic convergence or infinite sums of derivations are involved.

Terminal order is preserved: words with the same numbers of letters can have different values. Zeroness concerns the full function on words, not its commutative generating function or sums over word lengths. Cancellation between positive and negative tree weights is part of the semantics; there is no nonnegativity or probabilistic normalization promise.

All symbols and productions are listed explicitly with delimited binary indices. The algorithm is one ordinary deterministic Turing machine on finite descriptions, halting on every well-formed input and returning yes exactly for identically zero functions. No time bound is imposed; malformed descriptions can be rejected. The explicit binary normal form and coefficient field \(\mathbb{Q}\) are editorial choices fixing one benchmark variant.
cards.answer_criterion: A complete Lean-checked proof of a terminating decision algorithm for this rational weighted-grammar zeroness problem, or a Lean-checked undecidability proof. cards.definitions: The alphabet is a fixed finite disjoint union \(\Sigma=\Sigma_{\mathrm{call}}\cup\Sigma_{\mathrm{ret}}\cup\Sigma_{\mathrm{int}}\). A word is well-matched when every prefix has at least as many calls as returns and the whole word has equally many. A deterministic visibly pushdown automaton has finite control states, a finite stack alphabet with a bottom marker, an initial state and designated final states. It reads one letter per step, starting with just the bottom marker. A call pushes one non-bottom symbol, a return pops one symbol, and an internal letter leaves the stack unchanged; the finite transition table may inspect the state, letter and stack top. Acceptance requires a final control state and a stack containing just the bottom marker. Words that are not well-matched are rejected. Missing transitions reject. A language recognized by such an automaton is a visibly pushdown language (VPL); the automaton is fixed, while word length grows. Letters use a fixed-length injective binary code, and invalid codes are rejected. A nonuniform circuit family has one Boolean circuit for each input length, with no requirement that a machine generate the circuits. In \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\), circuits have polynomial size and constant depth and may use NOT and unbounded-fan-in AND, OR and majority gates. A majority gate returns one precisely when more than half its inputs are one. In \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\), circuits have polynomial size, depth \(O(\log(n+2))\), and AND and OR gates of fan-in at most two, together with NOT gates. Constants and polynomial exponents may depend on the fixed language. The reduction \(K\leq_{\mathrm{cd}}L\) consists of nonuniform constant-depth polynomial-size Boolean circuits with AND, OR and NOT gates and polynomial-length oracle gates for membership in \(L\). No directed path goes from an oracle output to an oracle input. The circuit decides \(K\), and its size includes the oracle-query wires. Completeness means \(L\in\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) and \(K\leq_{\mathrm{cd}}L\) for every \(K\in\mathrm{NC}^{1}\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated alternative for every VPL. Alternatively specify a VPL and prove in Lean both that it is outside \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\) and that it is not \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\)-hard under the stated reductions. The target does not additionally require an algorithm assigning automata to the alternatives. A classification using a different reduction or uniformity convention must establish that it implies this proposition.

context_blocks.text: The input itself prescribes when the machine uses its stack. Nested calls can therefore carry information that finite-state machines cannot store, while the matching structure remains visible before the control computation is performed. Well-matched words can nest arbitrarily deeply; the question does not impose a depth bound.

Every VPL is in \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\). The unresolved issue is whether any VPL occupies an intermediate position: requiring more than constant-depth threshold computation while failing to represent every logarithmic-depth bounded-fan-in computation. The known upper bound makes hardness and completeness equivalent here.

The 2024 paper classifies many VPLs relative to \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\), the constant-depth class without majority gates, and isolates a family whose \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) membership remains unresolved. That three-way outcome does not decide the present \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}/\mathrm{NC}^{1}\) question.

A lower bound against \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) is insufficient: majority and modular counting can require gates absent from \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) but still lie in \(\mathrm{TC}^{0}\). Conversely, knowing that a language has a logarithmic-depth circuit is only an upper bound, not a completeness proof.

The source separately asks whether membership in the threshold-circuit class can be decided from an automaton. This card selects the stated dichotomy proposition itself, preserving that distinction. It also retains the source’s constant-depth truth-table reductions, which allow several parallel oracle queries, rather than silently strengthening completeness to a single-query many-one reduction.

The two classes are not assumed to be different. If they coincide, the first alternative holds for every VPL. A negative answer would in particular separate them, so a conjectural class separation cannot be used as an unstated premise.

cards.title: Universality of unambiguous register automata over ordered integers
cards.formal:
Is universality decidable for unambiguous register automata with guessing over \((\mathbb Z,<,=)\) and finitely many named integer constants? Given a finite automaton description in the model below, promised to have at most one accepting run on every finite data word, must there be an algorithm deciding whether
\[L(\mathcal A)=(\Sigma\times\mathbb Z)^*?\]
The finite alphabet, number of registers, control states, guards and binary-encoded constants are all part of the input. This card makes the guessing convention explicit, using the relational register model discussed in the cited literature. Its main target is the decidability part of the source question; a tight complexity classification is a further question if the answer is positive.
cards.why: Unambiguity often preserves much of nondeterministic expressive power while recovering decidable equivalence or universality. This question tests that phenomenon over discrete ordered data with constants and guessed register values. Its resolution would identify how far the successful algorithms for equality and dense order extend toward integer-valued verification models.

cards.definitions:
The automaton has a finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\), a finite set of control states \(Q\), one initial state \(q_0\), a set \(F\subseteq Q\) of accepting states, and \(k\ge0\) registers with values in \(\mathbb Z\). All registers initially contain zero. This fixed initialization is part of the selected convention; integer constants, including zero, are available in guards. A data word is any finite sequence \((a_1,z_1)\cdots(a_m,z_m)\), where \(a_i\in\Sigma\) and \(z_i\in\mathbb Z\). The empty word is included.

For each control-state pair and input letter, the transition table specifies a quantifier-free Boolean formula \(g\) built using true, negation and conjunction from atoms \(u=v\) and \(u<v\). Terms \(u,v\) are the current input datum, an old register value \(r_i\), a proposed new register value \(r'_i\), or one of the finitely many integer constants in the description. Disjunction can be expressed using negation and conjunction. There is no addition, successor, multiplication or arbitrary numerical predicate in a guard. Parallel descriptions of the same transition relation are combined by disjunction.

From state \((q,\bar r)\) on input \((a,z)\), the automaton may move to any \((q',\bar r')\) for which the corresponding guard is true over the ordinary integers. Thus new register values may be nondeterministically guessed; they are not required to be copies of the input or old values. The transition relation may have infinitely many successors. Each transition consumes exactly one input letter, with no epsilon moves. A run is its sequence of control states and register tuples, starting at \((q_0,0,\ldots,0)\). It accepts if its control state after the last input letter is in \(F\). Acceptance depends on the existence of such a run, and no condition is imposed on final register contents. Different syntactic guard clauses producing the same sequence are not counted as different runs.

Unambiguity means that every word has at most one initialized accepting run, including all guessed values. There may be many rejecting or partial runs. In particular, a universal unambiguous automaton has exactly one accepting run for every word. This is a semantic promise on the supplied description, not a claim that all transition choices are unique.

Descriptions use finite binary encodings of states, letters, register indices, guard syntax and signed integer constants. A decision procedure is one deterministic Turing machine that halts and returns the correct universality answer on every description satisfying the promise. Its behavior on ambiguous or malformed descriptions is unrestricted, and it need not verify the promise. There is no complexity bound, bound on the number of registers, or bound on constant magnitudes beyond finiteness.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of decidability in this promised class, or prove that no such decision procedure exists. A positive answer must cover arbitrary finite register counts and named integer constants, with the specified guessing transitions. An undecidability reduction must produce unambiguous automata. Algorithms over rational data, over equality alone, or for a fixed restricted register model do not settle this integer-order target.

context_blocks.text: The source explicitly names the integers, their order and constants. Replacing them by the rationals changes the available values between two named constants. In addition, equality of control states does not identify runs with different guessed register tuples.

The relational guard convention follows the standard guessing model: guards constrain both old and new register values. Requiring every update to copy a previously seen datum would remove this feature. The card records this modeling choice explicitly because register-automaton terminology varies across papers.

Czerwiński, Mottet and Quaas establish decidability bounds in equality-based cases and for a one-register dense-order case. Their results do not state the general integer-order-with-constants theorem asked here.

The later vector-space approach gives exponential-time equivalence for unambiguous register automata with guessing over equality atoms and ordered atoms, and polynomial time at fixed register count. Its ordered atoms are the dense rational order. An appeal to that theorem alone does not establish universality over the discrete integer domain.

definitions: A finite timed word over a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\) is \((a_1,t_1)\cdots(a_n,t_n)\), where \(n\geq0\), \(a_i\in\Sigma\), and \(0\leq t_1\leq\cdots\leq t_n\) are real timestamps. Equal timestamps and the empty word are allowed.

A timed automaton has finite sets of locations \(Q\), clocks \(X\), initial locations \(I\subseteq Q\), final locations \(F\subseteq Q\), and transitions \((p,a,\phi,Y,q)\). Here \(a\in\Sigma\cup\{\varepsilon\}\), \(Y\subseteq X\), and \(\phi\) is a Boolean combination of true, false, \(x\mathrel{\sim} z\), and \(x-y\mathrel{\sim} z\), with clocks \(x,y\), integer \(z\), and \(\sim\in\{=,<,\leq,>,\geq\}\). There are no location invariants. All sets, transitions and guard formulas are explicitly encoded, with signed binary integer constants.

A run starts at time 0 in an initial location with all clocks zero. Time may advance by any nonnegative real amount, adding that amount to every clock. A transition can then fire when its guard is true; it changes the location and resets precisely the clocks in \(Y\) to zero. Its label and absolute firing time form an event. A finite run is accepting when its final location belongs to \(F\). The language \(L(A)\) consists of the timed words obtained from accepting runs by deleting all epsilon-labeled events and preserving the timestamps of all other events. Arbitrarily many but finitely many epsilon steps, including before the first and after the last visible event, are allowed.

A deterministic separator has exactly one initial location, no epsilon transitions, and at most one enabled transition for each location, input letter and clock valuation. Incomplete transition relations are permitted and a missing transition rejects. Equivalently one can merge overlapping guards when their target location and reset set coincide. The number of locations, number of clocks and magnitudes of constants can all depend on the input pair.

The decision algorithm is one ordinary deterministic Turing machine on the finite descriptions and must halt on every valid pair; no complexity bound or disjointness promise is imposed. A pair with intersecting languages necessarily has answer no. Malformed descriptions can be rejected.

cards.definitions: Fix a countably infinite set \(D\), whose elements have no structure except equality. A data word is a finite sequence \(w=d_1\cdots d_n\), including the empty word. A data permutation is a bijection \(D\to D\). The automaton consists of a state set \(Q\) acted on by all data permutations, an initial state \(q_0\) fixed by every permutation, a set of final states \(F\), and a total deterministic transition function \(\delta:Q\times D\to Q\). Both \(F\) and \(\delta\) are equivariant: renaming all data values preserves finality and commutes with transitions. Every state has finite support, meaning a finite set of data values whose pointwise fixation fixes the state. Orbit-finite means that renaming data partitions \(Q\) into finitely many equivalence classes. Acceptance starts at \(q_0\), follows the unique transition sequence and tests finality after the last letter. The finite input presentation is as follows. Each state orbit has an integer arity \(r\geq0\) and a finite subgroup \(H\) of the permutations of \(\{1,\ldots,r\}\). Its states are injective \(r\)-tuples of data, identified under coordinate permutations from \(H\). The presentation lists the orbit tags, arities, groups, final tags and a zero-arity initial tag. A finite transition table gives a target tag and a tuple of selectors from the old coordinates and current input datum for each possible equality case between that datum and the coordinates. These finite consistency conditions ensure a well-defined equivariant function; no unseen data value may be generated. There are no named data constants, data-order tests, predicates for arithmetic on positions or quantifiers over sets. Definability means that one finite sentence accepts exactly the language for all word lengths and all data values. cards.definitions: A configuration assigns one alphabet symbol to each lattice cell. A \(D\)-pattern is a function from \(D\) to \(A\), and distinct functions count as distinct patterns. The same allowed list \(P\) is enforced at every translate of \(D\); its entries need not all occur in a valid global configuration. The shape is arbitrary: it may be disconnected, nonconvex or contained in a proper sublattice. No rectangle, nearest-neighbor, connectedness or convexity assumption is imposed. A shift of finite type (SFT) is a set of configurations specified by finitely many forbidden finite patterns and all their translates. In the displayed presentation, the forbidden patterns are exactly \(A^D\setminus P\). The low-complexity restriction is on this finite allowed presentation, \(|P|\leq|D|\), not merely on the number of patterns observed in one chosen configuration. Periodic means invariant under at least one nonzero translation; two independent periods are not required in the proposition. An aperiodic SFT in the source’s terminology is nonempty and contains no configuration with even one nonzero period. All configurations and periods in the conclusion may depend on \(A,D,P\); no bound on a period’s size or running time of a construction is requested.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that every nonempty \(X(D,P)\) satisfying \(|P|\leq|D|\) contains a periodic configuration. Alternatively give explicit finite \(A,D,P\), prove the pattern-count bound and nonemptiness in Lean, and prove that every configuration in \(X(D,P)\) has no nonzero translation period. A nonperiodic member alone is not a counterexample, and a theorem restricted to convex shapes does not resolve the stated quantification.

context_blocks.text: A small set of local patterns can force large-scale regularity. If the shape consists of one cell, the bound permits at most one symbol, so every nonempty system is constant and periodic. Larger shapes can impose interacting constraints despite using at most as many allowed patterns as cells.

Kari and Moutot prove the implication for rectangular shapes in Corollary 5. Their conclusion extends the result to finite convex lattice shapes, meaning shapes containing all lattice points in their convex hull. The remaining question explicitly allows arbitrary shapes.

For the rectangular case, the existence of a periodic configuration also yields decidability of whether the finite local constraints admit any configuration; this is Corollary 6. General two-dimensional finite local constraints do not have this decidability property. The present card keeps periodic existence as its single main target.

Nivat’s conjecture makes a stronger demand about each individual configuration with few rectangular patterns: that configuration should itself be periodic. Here only one periodic member of the entire allowed system is required. An SFT can therefore satisfy this card even if it also has nonperiodic members.

The source describes why arbitrary scattered shapes are delicate. Such a shape may inspect only one parity class of lattice cells, allowing different sublattices to carry incompatible directions of periodicity. Known failures of an orbit-closure periodicity assertion for these shapes do not automatically supply a finite-type system with no periodic member.

The quantifier over all lattice cells matters. A collection of finite patches or a large computer-generated tiling does not by itself establish nonemptiness of an aperiodic SFT, nor does a search with no small period exclude every possible period.

cards.title: State complexity of complementing unambiguous automata
cards.formal: For each integer \(n\geq1\), define \[C(n)=\max_{A}\ \min\{\lvert Q_B\rvert: L(B)=\{0,1\}^{*}\setminus L(A)\},\] where \(A\) ranges over all unambiguous finite automata with between 1 and \(n\) states over the binary alphabet, and \(B\) ranges over nondeterministic finite automata over that alphabet with at least one state. definitions: Both kinds of automaton are finite tuples \((Q,\{0,1\},\Delta,I,F)\), where \(Q\) is the state set, \(I,F\subseteq Q\) are the initial and final state sets, and \(\Delta\subseteq Q\times\{0,1\}\times Q\) is a transition relation. Multiple initial states, missing transitions, unreachable states and empty initial or final sets are allowed. There are no epsilon transitions or duplicate parallel transitions.

An accepting run on a word \(a_1\cdots a_m\) is a state sequence \(q_0,\ldots,q_m\) with \(q_0\in I\), \(q_m\in F\), and \((q_{i-1},a_i,q_i)\in\Delta\) for every \(1\leq i\leq m\). A word belongs to the language if it has an accepting run. For the empty word the accepting runs are the states in \(I\cap F\). The input automaton is unambiguous when each word has at most one accepting run; there is no restriction on the number of rejecting runs.

Only the number of states is charged, not transitions, the alphabet description or computation used to construct the automaton. Up to state renaming there are finitely many eligible inputs. Determinization and complementation give an output with at most \(2^{n}\) states, so the minimum and maximum defining \(C(n)\) exist.

The target is a positive real-valued comparison function \(g\) on the positive integers, together with constants \(c_1,c_2>0\) and an integer \(n_0\geq1\), such that \(c_1g(n)\leq C(n)\leq c_2g(n)\) for every \(n\geq n_0\). Matching only the order of \(\log C(n)\) is weaker than this criterion. The function must specify an asymptotic rate rather than restate the defining automaton optimization.

cards.definitions: A word \(w=a_1\cdots a_n\) over a finite nonempty alphabet \(A\) is the finite structure on positions \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with position equality, order \(<\), and a unary letter predicate \(Q_a(i)\) for each \(a\in A\), true exactly when \(a_i=a\). Empty words have no positions. First-order formulas have Boolean connectives and quantifiers over positions only. The modular signature adds unary predicates \(M_{d,r}(i)\) meaning \(i\equiv r\pmod d\), and nullary predicates \(N_{d,r}\) meaning \(n\equiv r\pmod d\), for all integers \(d\geq1\) and \(0\leq r<d\). A formula uses finitely many of them, but there is no global modulus bound. These are position and length congruences, not quantifiers counting the number of positions satisfying a subformula. A fragment fixes either finitely many variable names or a countable list of names, and for every finite relational signature \(S\) specifies a set \(\mathcal F[S]\) of first-order formulas using those names. It contains all quantifier-free formulas on those variables and signatures, is closed under conjunction and disjunction, and is closed under quantifier-free substitution of relation atoms by formulas with the same available free variables, with bound variables renamed to avoid capture. Effectiveness here means one terminating procedure decides syntactic membership of a finite formula in \(\mathcal F[S]\) when its finite signature and formula are given. The names and arities of predicates and modular integers have ordinary finite encodings. For a signature with infinitely many available modular predicates, membership is read on the finite signature actually used. The notation \(\mathcal F[<]\) includes the letter and equality predicates, and \(\mathcal F[<,\mathrm{MOD}]\) also permits the modular predicates just defined. A deterministic finite automaton (DFA) is an explicit finite state set, initial state, final-state subset and total transition table on \(A\); it recognizes a regular language \(L\subseteq A^*\). Definability asks whether some sentence in the specified fragment has exactly language \(L\), for all finite words. Decidability means one deterministic Turing machine halting on every DFA/alphabet input. Its program may depend on the fixed fragment; no uniform transformation from base deciders to enriched deciders or running-time bound is required.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the implication for every effective fragment satisfying the specified closure conditions. Alternatively define a particular such fragment, prove its effectiveness and closure properties in Lean, give a Lean-verified algorithm for its base definability problem, and prove in Lean that the enriched definability problem is undecidable. Results about satisfiability, fixed moduli, separation given as an additional oracle, or only selected standard fragments do not decide this full implication.

context_blocks.text: The 2013 paper poses a general transfer question for fragments without providing one formal universe of admissible fragment descriptions. Editorial convention: the target above uses the quantifier-free-substitution closure framework made explicit in the 2019 follow-up literature, and additionally requires decidable syntax. This states a concrete transfer proposition; it is not presented as a verbatim formal theorem from the original concluding paragraph.

Adding congruence tests can increase expressive power while preserving regularity. For example, a nullary length predicate can require the whole word to have even length, and a unary predicate can restrict which letters occur at positions of a given parity. The question concerns whether a supplied regular language can be described at all, not whether an individual sentence has a model.

The 2013 theorem establishes decidability for two-variable first-order logic with modular predicates. Two-variable logic allows reusing two position-variable names under nested quantifiers. This important instance does not imply the universal transfer proposition for all admissible fragments.

cards.title: Unconditional containment of unambiguous probabilistic automata
cards.formal: Is quantitative containment decidable when the left automaton \(A\) is unambiguous and the right automaton \(B\) is finitely ambiguous? In other words, does a single unconditional terminating algorithm decide \(\forall w\in\Sigma^{*},\ p_A(w)\leq p_B(w)\) for every promised pair of rational probabilistic automata as defined below? This selects the direction of bounded-ambiguity containment whose known decidability proof uses Schanuel’s conjecture; the reverse direction is already decidable unconditionally.
cards.why: This asks whether a basic exact comparison between small stochastic models can be decided from a finite bound on accepting behavior, without a conjecture in transcendental number theory. The asymmetry between one probability product and a bounded sum isolates the unresolved arithmetic obstacle in an otherwise effective verification setting.

definitions: A probabilistic automaton is \(A=(\Sigma,Q,\delta,\iota,F)\), with a finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\), a finite nonempty state set \(Q\), accepting states \(F\subseteq Q\), nonnegative rational initial weights \(\iota(q)\) satisfying \(\sum_q\iota(q)\leq1\), and nonnegative rational transition weights \(\delta(q,a,p)\) satisfying \(\sum_p\delta(q,a,p)\leq1\) for each state \(q\) and letter \(a\). Missing probability mass is lost to rejection. There are no epsilon transitions. The input lists the states, alphabet, initial weights, accepting states and all nonzero transitions; rational numerators and positive denominators use binary notation.

For \(w=a_1\cdots a_m\), a positive accepting run is a state sequence \(q_0,\ldots,q_m\) with \(q_m\in F\) and \(\iota(q_0)\prod_{i=1}^{m}\delta(q_{i-1},a_i,q_i)>0\). Its weight is this product. Let \(p_A(w)\) be the sum of these weights. In particular \(p_A(\varepsilon)=\sum_{q\in F}\iota(q)\). Zero-weight transitions do not create runs; identical state-and-letter transitions are represented by one weight.

Unambiguous means at most one positive accepting run for each word. Finitely ambiguous means that there exists one integer \(K\geq0\), depending on the automaton but independent of the word and its length, such that every word has at most \(K\) positive accepting runs. This bound need not be supplied. Every finite word has finitely many runs even without the promise; a uniform bound over all words is the essential restriction.

Quantitative containment means exact pointwise comparison \(p_A(w)\leq p_B(w)\) for every finite word \(w\in\Sigma^{*}\), including the empty word. There is no cutpoint, approximation tolerance, isolated-gap promise, or bounded word length.

Decidability asks for one deterministic Turing machine on the finite descriptions, halting on every input string and outputting a bit. On each pair satisfying the stated structural promises, the bit must be 1 precisely for quantitative containment; outside the promise either bit is permitted. There is no time bound, oracle or unproved mathematical assumption in the requested result.
cards.answer_criterion: A complete Lean-checked proof of an unconditional decision algorithm for the stated promise problem, or a Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm exists. A proof conditional on Schanuel’s conjecture or on the decidability of real exponentiation is not sufficient. A procedure that only terminates when a violating word exists is not a decider.

cards.definitions:
For a finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\), a full binary labeled tree is a function \(t:\{0,1\}^*\to\Sigma\). The empty word is the root and the children of node \(u\) are \(u0,u1\). All branches are infinite.

A nondeterministic Muller tree automaton consists of a finite state set \(Q\), initial state \(q_0\), transition relation \(\Delta\subseteq Q\times\Sigma\times Q\times Q\), and an acceptance family \(\mathcal F\subseteq2^Q\). A run assigns a state to every node, starting with \(q_0\), and respects the transition relation at every node and its two children. It is accepting if, on each infinite branch, the set of states occurring infinitely often belongs to \(\mathcal F\). The language \(L(A)\) contains exactly the trees admitting at least one accepting run. No determinism, unambiguity or Borel-language promise is imposed.

In the Wadge game, Player I builds a tree over the alphabet of \(A\), and Player II builds one over the alphabet of \(B\). Both initially have empty finite trees. In each round I appends one or more complete levels, with all their labels, to I's own tree. II sees that move and appends finitely many complete levels to II's tree, or skips. Earlier labels cannot be changed. I therefore produces an infinite tree \(t\). II loses if II's output has only finitely many levels; otherwise it defines an infinite tree \(u\), and II wins exactly when
\[
t\in L(A)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u\in L(B).
\]
I wins in every other case. II may skip infinitely often, but must also extend the output infinitely often.

This is a perfect-information, length-\(\omega\), zero-sum game. A strategy specifies a legal move after every finite play history at which that player acts. A winning strategy succeeds against every legal opposing play. Strategies are arbitrary set-theoretic functions, with no computability, finite-memory or resource restriction. “Determined” means that one of the two players has a winning strategy.

The tree space has the product topology of discrete node labels: finitely many fixed levels specify basic neighborhoods. The tree-level version is the usual Wadge game; II has a winning strategy exactly when a continuous map \(F\) satisfies \(L(A)=F^{-1}(L(B))\). This equivalence explains the connection to language complexity, but does not assume determinacy.

The single sentence \(D_{\mathrm{tree}}\) universally quantifies over the finite automaton descriptions and asserts the existence of a winning strategy for each pair. The question asks whether ZFC proves that sentence. It does not assert that merely adding some stronger axiom is a negative resolution: such an axiom can prove statements already provable in ZFC.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive answer supplies a ZFC proof of determinacy for every pair in the specified class. A negative answer establishes nonprovability, for example by a relative-consistency or model construction yielding ZFC together with a failure of this universal determinacy statement; any metatheoretic consistency assumption must be stated explicitly. A theorem assuming a stronger determinacy principle without a nonprovability argument, or a proof for a restricted subclass, does not answer the ZFC-provability question.
